title: Kaur v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration)

How the layers nest here: The judge is the author (layer 1). The applicant and respondent in this proceeding make submissions to the judge (layer 2). The decision under review was made by an earlier decision-maker (layer 3), and that decision may itself report what a claimant, the Minister or a witness said to that decision-maker (layer 4).

paragraphs.text: The applicant is a 27-year-old citizen of India. She first came to Canada in September 2019 on a study permit to pursue a two-year Chemical Laboratory Technician Diploma at Sheridan College. After several extensions, the applicant’s study permit expired in July 2023. During the latter part of her studies, for various reasons, the applicant was unable to maintain her status as a full-time student. As a result, when she applied for a post-graduate work permit (PGWP), the application was refused.

In August 2024, the applicant applied for a temporary resident permit (TRP) under subsection 24(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 (IRPA). At the same time, she also requested an open work permit. The applicant explained that she was seeking a TRP to overcome her ineligibility for a PGWP because she wanted to obtain Canadian work experience.

In a decision dated February 17, 2025, an officer with Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada refused the application because the officer was not satisfied that a TRP was justified in the circumstances. In particular, the officer found that the applicant had not provided “sufficient documentation to prove that [she] would experience difficulty should [she] be expected to return to [her] home country in order to regularize [her] status, and re-apply for a [work permit].”

The applicant seeks judicial review of this decision under subsection 72(1) of the IRPA on the basis that the decision is unreasonable. As I will explain, I am not persuaded that there is any basis to interfere with the decision.

The parties agree, as do I, that the merits of the officer’s decision should be reviewed on a reasonableness standard (Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 at para 10). A reasonable decision “is one that is based on an internally coherent and rational chain of analysis and that is justified in relation to the facts and law that constrain the decision maker” (Vavilov, at para 85).

When conducting reasonableness review, a reviewing court must take a “reasons first” approach that examines and evaluates the justification the administrative decision maker has given for its decision, always bearing in mind the history of the proceeding and the administrative context in which the decision was made (Mason v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2023 SCC 21 at paras 58-60). The reviewing court must read the decision maker’s reasons “holistically and contextually” (Vavilov, at para 97) and in light of “the evidence before the decision maker, the submissions of the parties, publicly available policies or guidelines that informed the decision maker’s work, and past decisions of the relevant administrative body” (Vavilov, at para 94).

To set aside a decision on the basis that it is unreasonable, the reviewing court must be satisfied that “there are sufficiently serious shortcomings in the decision such that it cannot be said to exhibit the requisite degree of justification, intelligibility and transparency” (Vavilov, at para 100).

Subsection 24(1) of the IRPA provides that an officer may issue a TRP to a foreign national who is inadmissible to Canada or who does not meet the requirements of the Act if the officer is of the opinion that doing so “is justified in the circumstances.” It is well established that the objective of this provision is to provide flexibility in situations where a strict application of the IRPA would result in undue hardship because there are compelling reasons to allow a foreign national to enter or remain in Canada despite their inadmissibility or non-compliance with the Act: see Farhat v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2006 FC 1275 at para 22; and Ogbonna v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2024 FC 1467 at paras 19-29.

In my view, it was open to the officer to conclude that the applicant had not established that issuing a TRP was justified in the circumstances. The burden was on the applicant to demonstrate that she had a compelling reason to be allowed to remain in Canada despite her inadmissibility. Critically, the officer found that a TRP was not justified because the applicant could regularize her status from India and she had not provided any evidence that she would “experience difficulty” if she were required to do so. I do not agree with the applicant that the officer has imported some sort of hardship-based test. Rather, the officer was simply considering whether there was a compelling need for a TRP given that other options for achieving the outcome the applicant sought – the ability to obtain work experience in Canada – were reasonably open to the applicant.

While the officer’s analysis is somewhat cursory, the central point is clear: since the applicant had not demonstrated that she did not have other viable options for obtaining Canadian work experience, she had not demonstrated a compelling reason to be allowed to remain in Canada on a TRP in order to obtain that experience. Given the information before the officer, this was an altogether reasonable conclusion. Since this was determinative of the TRP application, there was no need for the officer to say more about why a TRP was not justified in the circumstances. The officer’s reasons are brief but they are transparent and intelligible. Most importantly, when read in the context of the record before the officer, the statutory requirements, and the governing jurisprudence, they justify the result.

The applicant’s circumstances are sympathetic and her desire to obtain work experience in Canada is understandable. While she must have been disappointed by the officer’s decision, she has not demonstrated that it is unreasonable. This application for judicial review must, therefore, be dismissed.

The parties did not propose any serious questions of general importance for certification under paragraph 74(d) of the IRPA. I agree that no question arises. JUDGMENT IN IMM-5153-25 THIS COURT’S JUDGMENT is that The application for judicial review is dismissed.
